newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: EU clears Bank Austria/Creditanstalt merger.
newsitem.headline: EU clears Bank Austria/Creditanstalt merger.

text.p: The European Commission on Monday approved Bank Austria's takeover of rival Creditanstalt, clearing the way for the creation a new Austrian banking giant with total assets of more than 1,300 billion schillings ($108 billion).
The combined bank will be more than five times the size of its closest domestic rival, but will still only rank 30th among Europe's top banks.

"The commission has approved the acquisition of majority control of Creditanstalt by Bank Austria after assurances were made which will remove concerns about competition issues," the Commission said in a statement.

The hard-won merger of Bank Austria and Creditanstalt, one-time banker to the Habsburg family of Austro-Hungarian emperors, was Europe's longest running privatisation project and threatened to bring down Austria's coalition government of dominant Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party.

The conservatives, afraid of losing blue-blooded Creditanstalt to Social-Democrat controlled Bank Austria, gave up their fight only after winning assurances that the bank would be taken out of public control and that Creditantstalt would remain an independent entity for at least five years.
The Commission had started a probe into the privatisation of Creditanstalt in February under the European Union's merger rules which ban the creation or strengthening of dominant positions.
Nobody at Bank Austria, which won the bid to take over the Austrian state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt in January, was immediately available for comment.

The Commission said the 17.2 billion schilling merger had raised concerns about the bank's almost complete dominance of Austria's sheltered financial sector, particularly in the areas of private banking and securities clearing.
"The Austrian banking markets are...marked by obstacles to new entrants, so that the danger of the creation of or the increase in an already dominant market position was posed," the commission said.

Brussels had approved the deal on condition that the combined bank sell its stake in savings bank GiroCredit, and reduce its stakes in export financing agent Kontrollbank and Investkredit, which is active in municipal financing, it said.
The GiroCredit stake is held by the City of Vienna's Anteilverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation, which also effectively controls Bank Austria.

Bank Austria and AVZ last week agreed to sell their 56 percent stake in GiroCredit to savings bank Die Erste. No details of the deal, reportedly worth some 8.2 billion schillings, have been made public.

As part of January's merger agreement, AVZ is obliged to reduce its stake in Bank Austria to below 25 percent over a period of five years. The Austrian state's 19 percent stake in the bank will be sold via the bourse this year.

The Commission also required Bank Austria to reduce its dominant position in the domestic construction industry. It said the bank had agreed to sell its stake in market leader Universale, previously held by Creditanstalt, or alternatively to sell its stake in construction group Stuag.
